tldr: To enable robotic simulation of everyday soft objects, this study builds RFW-S—a dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified deformable assets derived from 100,000 3D models via structure-aware physical modeling, LLM-assisted property estimation, and independent simulation verification under stimuli distinct from parameter calibration.
hero_caption: Overall construction pipeline of RFW-S. After generating 3D geometry from images, the pipeline adapts models into physical representations suited to each structural family and calibrates parameters through simulated drop tests. Once candidates are frozen, they undergo independent verification via lateral compression tests and runtime contract checks, admitting only high-quality assets.
overview:
When robots operate in homes or workplaces, physical interaction with deformable objects—such as squeezing a sponge, folding a towel, or lifting a tote bag—is unavoidable. Training and evaluating these tasks in simulation requires a massive volume of diverse, physically grounded 3D assets. However, existing large-scale 3D datasets focus primarily on visual diversity. Many are not executable in physics engines, or they simply assign arbitrary stiffness values that lead to unnatural collapse or simulation explosion.

To address this, the authors developed RFW-S, a large-scale dataset covering everyday deformable objects. Starting with 100,000 initial models across 485 categories generated via generative AI, the pipeline converts them into appropriate physical representations (PBD or MPM) based on structural features—such as solid interiors or open-mouthed bags. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) estimate physical parameters, which are then automatically calibrated based on drop test behaviors in simulation.

The key novelty of this work is independent simulation verification: evaluating assets under interactions completely distinct from those used for calibration. Tuning parameters to pass a drop test does not guarantee an object will survive being squeezed from the sides. After calibration, the asset configurations are fully frozen and subjected to an independent compression-release test. Remarkably, about 4% of the models that passed calibration failed this independent test, highlighting the necessity of independent verification.

Ultimately, 83,365 verified assets survived, covering all 485 categories. Furthermore, robotic grasping experiments revealed a stark gap between task success and object integrity—robots often lifted an object successfully while destroying it internally. A sim-to-real replay experiment grasping tofu on a physical robot faithfully reproduced the exact boundary between structural failure and intact transport observed in simulation.
contributions: Constructed RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified deformable assets spanning 485 everyday categories and five structural families.

Developed an automated construction pipeline integrating structure-aware geometric adaptation (considering internal fill and open boundaries), MLLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration, and post-freeze independent verification.

Quantified the divergence between grasp task success and object integrity (non-destruction) in robotic grasping, and validated the real-world fidelity of simulated behaviors through sim-to-real experiments on fragile tofu.

sections.heading: Why Isn't Visual Fidelity Enough for Deformable Simulation?
sections.summary: Operating deformable objects is vital for robots in everyday environments, yet executable simulation-ready assets remain scarce. Simply assigning stiffness values to meshes is inadequate; models require structure-aware physical representations and behavioral verification under stimuli distinct from calibration.
sections.details:
Consider everyday robotic tasks. Squeezing a sponge compresses it, dropping a towel makes it drape, and lifting a tote bag causes its handles and pouch to fold. Contact-induced deformations directly determine not only whether a grasp succeeds, but also whether the object survives without damage.

Simulators enable safe, large-scale robot learning, but existing 3D asset libraries focus heavily on visual appearance and surface geometry. Very few can be executed in physics engines. Moreover, deformable simulation is far more delicate than rigid-body simulation. A solid cushion needs internal volume, while a bag requires an open boundary. Without appropriate structural representations, adjusting material parameters such as Young's modulus will never yield realistic dynamics.

A further complication is that an asset may behave plausibly in one scenario but fail completely in another. For example, an object might look convincing during free-fall impact onto the floor, but its mesh might invert or explode when poked laterally by a finger.

To tackle this problem, the authors introduce RFW-S (RoboFlyWheel-Soft). Starting from 100,000 generated assets, the pipeline applies structure adaptation and LLM-assisted parameter calibration, freezes the configurations, and performs independent simulation verification under alternative stimuli. This yields 83,365 high-quality, verified everyday deformable models.

sections.heading: How Does RFW-S Differ from Existing 3D Asset Repositories?
sections.summary: While large-scale datasets like Objaverse offer rich visual diversity, they lack physical verification. Environments dedicated to garments or specific tasks exist, but RFW-S is the first to cover diverse everyday deformable categories with independent behavioral verification.
sections.details:
### 3D Asset Generation and Physical Environments
Recent years have seen the emergence of multi-million-scale 3D repositories such as Objaverse-XL, along with physics-verified rigid-body datasets for robotics like ManiTwin. In deformable domains, garment-focused datasets like CLOTH3D and GarmentLab, as well as manipulation environments such as SoftGym and PlasticineLab, have also been actively developed.

However, these collections are either restricted to narrow domains (e.g., only garments or only clay) or lack visual variation. A broad library covering general everyday categories with guaranteed physical behaviors has been missing.

### Parameter Estimation and Simulation Feedback
Growing research explores predicting physical properties such as Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from images or videos (e.g., PUGS and various LLM-based approaches), as well as system identification from real-world video (e.g., Vid2Sid). This work also leverages MLLM priors for initial estimation, but sets itself apart by running an automated diagnostic feedback loop in simulation and enforcing a separate, independent evaluation test.

### Fragile Object Manipulation and Damage Assessment
In deformable object grasping, prior work often evaluated only whether an object was lifted without dropping. However, for fragile objects like tofu or cake, excessive grip force crushes the item. This paper introduces an integrity metric based on the deformation gradient, establishing a framework that separates task success from structural integrity.

sections.heading: 83,365 Verified Assets: What Is Inside RFW-S?
sections.summary: RFW-S spans 485 everyday categories across five structural families, derived from an initial pool of 100,000 assets down to 83,365 that passed rigorous physical verification and contract checks. Visual meshes, physical proxies, and execution logs are fully cataloged.
sections.details:
### Broad Coverage Across Four Structural Levels
The dataset covers 485 everyday categories grouped into five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. The initial pool generated an evenly distributed 100,000 assets, roughly 206 to 207 per category.

To ensure rigorous analysis, the paper strictly distinguishes four operational units:
- **Category**: Semantic object type (e.g., cupcake, tote bag)
- **Asset**: A generated object with a unique identifier
- **Configuration**: A complete set of geometry, simulation representation, physical parameters, and solver settings
- **Episode**: A single interaction trial executing a configuration

### Decoupling Visual Meshes from Physical Proxies
A crucial design decision is separating rendering meshes from physical proxies. Visual meshes for CG rendering and physical proxies (particles or simplified meshes) used by physics engines (PBD or MPM) possess different topologies. RFW-S records full mappings among reference images, visual meshes, physical proxies, effective simulation parameters, and constraints.

### Surviving Two Rigorous Filters
All 100,000 assets were subjected to runtime/behavioral contract (RC) checks (ensuring simulation completes without numerical explosion) and physical verification (evaluating plausible deformation and recovery). While 16,221 assets passed RC only and 253 passed physical verification only, exactly 83,365 assets (83.37% of the initial pool) satisfied both criteria simultaneously to become official RFW-S assets. Importantly, verified assets survived across every one of the 485 categories.

captions.F3: Lifecycle of a sunshade-fabric asset. From the reference image, visual meshes and physical proxies are generated, retaining execution records passing both drop calibration and lateral compression independent testing (deformation ratio 0.208, recovery ratio 0.968).

sections.heading: From Asset Generation to Verification: How LLMs and Physics Engines Cooperate
sections.summary: Initial geometries are generated using image and 3D generative AI, then adapted into structure-specific physical representations. An MLLM estimates initial parameters, calibrates them via drop probes, and the frozen configuration is tested under an independent compression probe.
sections.details:
### Structure-Aware Geometric Adaptation
First, reference images generated by Qwen-Image-2.0 guide 3D mesh creation via TRELLIS.2. Next comes structure adaptation. For instance, a beanbag cushion filled with beads is converted to an internally voxel-filled MPM (Material Point Method) representation, whereas an empty cloth tote bag requires an open-boundary PBD (Position-Based Dynamics) shell representation. The pipeline automatically fixes non-manifold edges, repairs double vertices, and fills internal volumes.

For garments, raw 3D meshes often contain strong curvature support that preserves their upright generation pose. Without intervention, they remain stiff like mannequins regardless of softness settings. The pipeline applies a compliant cloth profile that intentionally lowers curvature resistance to allow natural draping.

### MLLM Property Estimation and Calibration Loop
Once geometry is established, a multimodal model (Qwen3.8-max) estimates initial properties $\theta_0$ (density, Young's modulus, yield stress, etc.) from images and category names. These map to effective solver parameters $\theta_{\rm eff}$. The asset enters a free-fall drop probe onto the floor. The simulator diagnoses contact occurrence, numerical divergence, deformation scale, and post-bounce resting states. If anomalies occur, diagnostic text is fed back to the LLM to adjust parameters iteratively.

### Freezing Configurations for Independent Verification
This is the core contribution of the pipeline. Once calibration yields a passing candidate, its geometry, physical representation, parameters, and solver settings are completely frozen. The model is then subjected to a single-shot independent verification probe—a lateral compression and release test—applying forces entirely distinct from the drop test.

Pass/fail criteria (admissible bands for compression and recovery ratios) were statistically determined through a study where 10 robotics experts evaluated 150 simulation video clips. Only assets clearing this independent trial are officially adopted.

captions.F6: Physics authoring and verification workflow. The calibration loop on the left refines parameters using diagnostic text. Once frozen, candidate configurations proceed to independent verification (right) under an alternative probe test, where pass/fail is decided in a single shot without further tuning.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Why Tuning Alone Fails and How Independent Verification Proves Its Value
sections.summary: Garment experiments demonstrate the necessity of structural adaptation, while 8,400 trials confirm that independent verification catches failures hidden during calibration. Grasping and sim-to-real tofu experiments further confirm the physical realism of the simulated assets.
sections.details:
### Family-Wise Coverage and Challenging Categories
Of the initial 100,000 assets, the physical verification pass rate was 83.62%, the RC check pass rate was 99.59%, and their intersection was 83.37%. By family, cloth sheets achieved a 98.46% pass rate, whereas soft solids reached 60.92%. Highly compliant, viscous food categories—such as gummy candy (3 of 206 passed) and raw chocolate (9 of 206 passed)—frequently over-deformed or suffered numerical instabilities under current simulator models.

### Garment Deformation: Parameter Tuning vs. Structural Adaptation
Testing four garment models under three configurations ('shape-preserving', 'soft material', and 'compliant cloth with structural adaptation') revealed striking differences. Simply softening material parameters barely lowered the normalized height ratio after impact (from 0.499 to 0.470). In contrast, the compliant cloth profile with relaxed curvature resistance collapsed to 0.312, naturally creasing and crumpling like real fabric. Geometric intervention is indispensable alongside parameter tuning.

### Does Independent Verification Truly Matter?
Across 300 bag assets tested under multiple methods and budgets (8,400 total runs), all configurations had cleared prior drop calibration. However, 325 runs (3.87%) subsequently failed the independent compression test. Passing a calibration probe does not guarantee plausible behavior under alternative interactions.

### Grasp Success vs. Object Integrity Trade-Off
Robotic grasping, lifting, and holding experiments were conducted across 1,000 instances from seven base geometries. A damage metric $D$ computed from deformation gradient tensors $F$ flagged damage when $D \ge 0.25$. Across 4,000 grasping trials, lifting succeeded 3,079 times, but every single trial triggered the damage flag—yielding zero 'intact success' cases. Firmly gripping an object to prevent slippage easily crushes soft interiors, illustrating the fundamental challenge of deformable manipulation.

### Sim-to-Real Tofu Grasping
To verify whether simulated fragility matches reality, real-world grasping experiments were performed on a Piper robot arm using fresh tofu blocks. Gripper width commands corresponding to 'excessive squeeze leading to fracture' and 'compliant grasp enabling intact transport' were generated in simulation and replayed on the physical robot. The physical tofu fractured or transported cleanly at the exact boundaries predicted by simulation, confirming that the physical properties capture real-world failure thresholds.

captions.F7: Comparison of garment (trousers) drop behavior. The shape-preserving setting (top) and simple soft material setting (middle) retain an unnatural upright posture. Only the compliant cloth profile (bottom) allows the garment to collapse naturally onto the floor.
captions.F10: Sim-to-real replay comparison of tofu grasping between the Piper arm and MPM simulation. (a) Excessive squeeze causes tofu fracture and dropping in both simulation and reality. (b) Appropriate gripper width successfully transports the tofu intact to the plate in both environments.

sections.heading: Where Does RFW-S Stand and What Challenges Remain?
sections.summary: While RFW-S delivers executable models across 485 everyday categories, limitations remain in modeling viscoelastic extremes, decoupling rigid rotation from deformation metrics, and anchoring simulation parameters directly to real-world mechanical measurements.
sections.details:
### Coverage and Representation Boundaries
Although verified models exist for all 485 categories, pass rates dropped sharply for items with extreme plasticity or viscosity, such as soft candy and ganache. Current PBD and MPM implementations in Genesis lack dedicated constitutive parameters to capture these complex material regimes fully.

### Limitations of the Integrity Metric
The deformation gradient-based damage metric $D$ used in grasping tests is sensitive to rigid-body rotation as well as strain. Part of the 100% damage flag rate in grasping trials likely stems from rotational components as objects tilted in the gripper. Future evaluations will require rotation-invariant strain measures.

### Grounding to Real-World Physical Measurements
While sim-to-real tofu trials showed strong agreement, the tens of thousands of assets in the dataset are not calibrated against physical force-displacement or tensile test measurements. Continual validation is needed to map effective simulation parameters to standard SI mechanical units.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A New Foundation for Everyday Deformable Simulation
sections.summary: RFW-S provides 83,365 simulation-verified everyday deformable assets with full execution logs. Combining structure-aware modeling with independent verification establishes a trustworthy simulation foundation for deformable robotic manipulation.
sections.details:
Starting from 100,000 generated assets, RFW-S produced 83,365 verified deformable models across 485 categories by combining structure-aware proxy adaptation, LLM-guided parameter estimation and calibration, and independent simulation verification under alternative stimuli.

Key takeaways from this work—that material tuning requires structural adaptation, that calibration does not guarantee robustness without independent verification, and that grasp success must be separated from structural damage—provide crucial principles for embodied AI and deformable manipulation.

Future research directions include extending the pipeline to articulated-deformable hybrid objects and integrating generative models for interactive 4D scene synthesis.

sections.heading: Appendix: Expert Validation Studies and Detailed Setup
sections.summary: The appendix details the 10-expert video evaluation study establishing acceptance thresholds, solver routing statistics across families, and controller designs for robotic grasping experiments.
sections.details:
### Expert Realism Evaluation Study
To determine pass/fail bands for deformation and recovery ratios, 10 robotics experts scored 150 representative simulation video clips (75 drop, 75 compression) on a 5-point scale. This study identified boundaries where humans perceive an object as stably at rest even if residual velocity is non-zero, yielding realistic acceptance thresholds rather than over-penalizing benign numerical drift.

### Automated Solver Routing
An inspection of solver modes across 300 sampled assets showed that cloth sheets and garments routed almost 100% to PBD-cloth, while soft solids predominantly routed to elastoplastic-MPM. Shells and bags routed dynamically between PBD and MPM depending on whether their interiors were hollow or filled.

### Grasping Controller Configurations
Grasping evaluations tested three controllers: fixed-width, slip-feedback, and local force-prior grasping, alongside a privileged reference controller selecting the best outcome across five trials using ground-truth damage feedback. While task success rates were high, none achieved zero damage under the strict integrity threshold, underscoring the challenge of delicate soft-body force control.

captions.F12: Detailed verification statistics from the appendix. (a) Final status of 100,000 assets (83,292 passed initially, 326 passed after revision), (b) additional stability checks on 2,000 bags, (c) solver assignment distribution across families, and (d) realism rating score distributions from 150 expert-evaluated clips.

takeaways: Simulating deformable objects requires structure-aware adaptation—such as interior volume filling, open boundaries, and reducing artificial curvature resistance—not just adjusting material stiffness parameters.

Passing a calibration test (e.g., drop impact) does not prevent failure under different contact modes (e.g., compression); independent verification with frozen configurations is vital for physical reliability.
In robotic grasping of soft objects, task success (lifting without dropping) diverges sharply from object integrity (avoiding crushing), making explicit damage-aware control and evaluation essential.
limitations: The deformation gradient-based damage metric $D$ incorporates rigid-body rotation alongside strain, causing nearly all grasped objects to trigger damage flags and obscuring comparisons of intact success.
Assets with extreme viscoelasticity or plasticity (e.g., gummy candy or raw chocolate) suffer low verification pass rates due to the expressive limits of current simulator solvers.
Sim-to-real physical validation is demonstrated on select cases like tofu grasping, but the dataset lacks ground-truth mechanical measurements (e.g., tensile tests) across all 485 categories.
